concept.name: Microservices Decomposition

relationships.description: Connects Microservices Decomposition to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Split a system along business capability and transactional consistency boundaries, not technical layers or entity nouns.
spark.keyTakeaway: If two services must update state together synchronously on every write, they belong in the same service boundary until you can decouple them with an outbox and asynchronous events.

concept.whyItMatters: Premature or poorly aligned service boundaries turn fast in-memory method calls into 2–10 ms network hops, replace ACID transactions with distributed sagas, and force teams into lockstep deployments. Proper decomposition aligns service ownership with independent release cadences, isolated failure domains, and distinct scaling profiles.
whenToUse: Distinct subsystems have sharply different scaling or hardware profiles (e.g., CPU-bound checkout at 200 QPS vs. read-heavy catalog search at 25,000 QPS).
Multiple autonomous teams (6–8 engineers each) experience merge conflicts, shared CI bottlenecks, and coupled release trains in a single codebase.
Regulatory or fault-isolation requirements demand strict blast-radius containment (e.g., isolating PCI-DSS payment card processing from general user profiles).
whenNotToUse: Early-stage products or unvalidated domains where entity boundaries shift weekly and cross-cutting schema refactors are frequent.
Small engineering teams (fewer than 15–20 engineers) where Kubernetes, service mesh, and distributed tracing overhead outweighs deployment independence.
Ultra-low-latency trading or real-time game loops (<5 ms end-to-end budget) where serialization and network hops break SLAs.
keyPoints: Align boundaries to Domain-Driven Design (DDD) bounded contexts discovered via Event Storming rather than CRUD entity tables.
Enforce database-per-service ownership; sharing a single PostgreSQL schema across services creates a distributed monolith with hidden coupling.
Use the Strangler Fig pattern at an edge proxy (Envoy or Kong) to route specific paths to extracted services incrementally without a big-bang rewrite.
Replace distributed two-phase commit (2PC) with the Transactional Outbox pattern (Debezium CDC + Kafka) and idempotent consumers.
Bound synchronous call depth to <=2 hops on critical paths to prevent tail-latency amplification and availability collapse.

examples.title: E-Commerce Checkout Extraction via Strangler Fig
examples.scenario: A 450k-LOC Rails monolith suffered 45-minute CI queues and Black Friday checkout stalls whenever catalog indexing spiked database CPU to 95%.
examples.outcome: Routing `/api/v2/checkout/*` through Envoy to a standalone Go/PostgreSQL Order service and publishing `OrderPlaced` events via Debezium CDC cut checkout p99 latency from 840 ms to 115 ms and enabled 12x independent daily deploys.

examples.title: Over-Granular Entity Service Consolidation
examples.scenario: A fintech team split `User`, `Address`, `KycStatus`, and `AccountTier` into four separate gRPC microservices, requiring 4 sequential RPCs per login.
examples.outcome: Merging them back into a single Identity bounded context eliminated 3 network hops per request, reduced p99 login latency from 92 ms to 18 ms, and removed 4 separate Helm charts and on-call rotations.

tradeOffs.pro: Teams ship, scale, and roll back services independently without coordinating a monolith release train.
tradeOffs.con: Requires service discovery, mTLS (Istio/Linkerd), distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), and per-service CI/CD pipelines.

tradeOffs.pro: A memory leak or CPU spike in Recommendations cannot crash the Checkout database connection pool.
tradeOffs.con: A synchronous chain of 5 services each with 99.9% availability yields 99.5% composite availability and additive p99 tail latency.

tradeOffs.pro: Each service picks its optimal store (e.g., Elasticsearch for search, PostgreSQL for ledger, Redis for sessions).
tradeOffs.con: Cross-service joins disappear, forcing eventual consistency, saga compensation logic, and read-model projections.

failureModes.name: Distributed Monolith (Temporal Coupling)
failureModes.description: Services require synchronized deployments because breaking changes in gRPC/JSON schemas or shared database tables ripple across 6+ services.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce backward-compatible Protobuf/Avro schema evolution via a Schema Registry and forbid cross-service database reads.

failureModes.name: Chatty RPC Fan-Out & Retry Storms
failureModes.description: An aggregator fires 30 sequential N+1 HTTP/gRPC calls per request; a 50 ms downstream hiccup triggers retries that multiply traffic 4x.
failureModes.mitigation: Batch endpoints, cache read projections locally, cap retry budgets at 10% of traffic, and use Envoy circuit breakers.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write State Divergence
failureModes.description: A service commits to PostgreSQL and then crashes before publishing the corresponding Kafka event, leaving downstream billing permanently out of sync.
failureModes.mitigation: Write domain events to an `outbox` table in the same local ACID transaction and stream them asynchronously via Debezium CDC.

failureModes.name: Nano-Service Proliferation
failureModes.description: Splitting every CRUD table into its own microservice bloats infrastructure cost and cognitive load faster than team headcount grows.
failureModes.mitigation: Require a minimum team-ownership ratio (at most 1–2 services per 2-pizza team) and coalesce tightly coupled entities.

commonMistakes: Decomposing by technical layer (UI service, API service, DB service) instead of vertical business capabilities.
Allowing multiple services to read and write the same relational database tables.
Performing cross-service joins synchronously in API gateways instead of maintaining materialized CQRS read views.
Skipping distributed correlation IDs (`traceparent` W3C header) until after a production outage.
Extracting the most coupled core domain first instead of starting with decoupled edge capabilities like Notifications.

sections.content:
## The idea

Microservices decomposition is the discipline of partitioning a monolithic system into independently deployable, network-isolated services aligned with **Domain-Driven Design (DDD) bounded contexts**. Rather than slicing by technical tier or individual database tables, you group data and behavior that change for the same business reason and require immediate transactional invariants. Each service owns its private data store, exposes a versioned contract (gRPC/Protobuf or REST/OpenAPI), and communicates cross-boundary state changes asynchronously over an event log such as Apache Kafka.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider extracting an **Orders** service from a legacy e-commerce monolith handling 3,000 RPS:

1. **Map Events & Invariants**: Use Event Storming to identify that `Order`, `OrderLineItem`, and `IdempotencyKey` share a strict ACID invariant, whereas `EmailReceipt` and `LoyaltyPoints` can lag by 500 ms.
2. **Introduce Edge Routing**: Place an Envoy proxy in front of the monolith. Mirror 5% of `POST /orders` traffic (shadowing) to the new Orders service to validate parity without impacting users.
3. **Establish Private Storage & CDC**: Provision a dedicated PostgreSQL instance for Orders with an `outbox_events` table. When `POST /orders` commits, it inserts both the order row and the `OrderCreated` outbox row in one transaction.
4. **Shift Traffic & Cut Over**: Shift production `POST /orders` weight in Envoy from 0% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%, while Debezium tails PostgreSQL WAL logs to publish `OrderCreated` to Kafka for Loyalty and Notifications.

sections.content:
## Boundary heuristics & coupling metrics

Good boundaries minimize **afferent/efferent network coupling** while maximizing **functional cohesion** within each service. Track three quantitative signals before splitting:

- **Change Coupling (Git Co-change)**: If `ServiceA` and `ServiceB` are modified together in >40% of pull requests over 90 days, their boundary is drawn in the wrong place.
- **Composite SLA Math**: If a request fans out synchronously across $k$ services each with availability $A = 0.999$, composite availability drops to $A^k$ (e.g., $0.999^{10} \approx 99.0\%$, or 7.3 hours of downtime/month).
- **Data Ownership Ratio**: Every table must have exactly one writer service; any cross-service read must use an API or an asynchronous Kafka-backed projection.

## Decomposition strategies compared

| Strategy | Primary Axis | Best Fit | Latency Impact | Rollback Difficulty |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **DDD Bounded Context** | Domain language & invariants | Core business domains (Orders, Billing) | Low (few cross-context hops) | Medium (requires data migration) |
| **Strangler Fig** | Edge URL / gRPC method | Incremental legacy monolith extraction | Neutral during shadow; low post-cutover | Low (flip Envoy route weights back) |
| **Volatility-Based** | Rate of requirement change | Separating stable ledger from rapid promo rules | Low-Medium | Medium |
| **Scaling / SLA Split** | QPS, CPU/GPU, or compliance | Isolating ML inference or PCI-DSS vault | High if synchronous; low if async | Low |

## Failure modes

Production microservice migrations most often fail at the **network and state boundaries**:

- **Cascading Timeout Collapse**: Without explicit deadline propagation (`grpc-timeout`), a slow downstream query exhausts upstream worker threads across every caller.
- **Saga Compensation Bugs**: Long-running distributed sagas (e.g., `ReserveInventory -> ChargeCard -> Fail`) often leave orphaned reservations when compensating actions are not idempotent.
- **Schema Drift**: Unversioned JSON payloads break consumers silently when optional fields become required.

## Production hardening

Harden every extracted boundary before shifting 100% traffic:

- **Contract Testing**: Run Pact or Buf breaking-change checks in CI so a provider cannot merge an incompatible Protobuf/OpenAPI change.
- **Deadlines & Circuit Breakers**: Enforce strict per-hop timeouts (e.g., 150 ms) and Envoy outlier detection (eject hosts after 5 consecutive 5xx responses).
- **Idempotency Keys**: Require a client-generated `Idempotency-Key` UUID on all mutating endpoints and deduplicate Kafka consumers via a `processed_events` table.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify each proposed service maps to a single DDD bounded context owned by one 2-pizza team.
- [ ] Confirm zero shared database tables or cross-service SQL joins exist.
- [ ] Implement the Transactional Outbox + Debezium CDC for all state-to-event emissions.
- [ ] Cap synchronous intra-request call depth at <=2 hops with propagated gRPC/HTTP deadlines.
- [ ] Wire OpenTelemetry W3C `traceparent` headers and per-service SLO burn-rate alerts before cutover.

interviewProblems.title: Microservices Decomposition
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Microservices Decomposition. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Split a system along business capability and transactional consistency boundaries, not technical layers or entity nouns.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Orders Service + PG applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Debezium + Kafka.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Debezium + Kafka experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce backward-compatible Protobuf/Avro schema evolution via a Schema Registry and forbid cross-service database reads.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: If two services must update state together synchronously on every write, they belong in the same service boundary until you can decouple them with an outbox and asynchronous events.
Avoid trap: Decomposing by technical layer (UI service, API service, DB service) instead of vertical business capabilities.
Avoid trap: Allowing multiple services to read and write the same relational database tables.
When to reach for it: Distinct subsystems have sharply different scaling or hardware profiles (e.g., CPU-bound checkout at 200 QPS vs. read-heavy catalog search at 25,000 QPS).
When to reach for it: Multiple autonomous teams (6–8 engineers each) experience merge conflicts, shared CI bottlenecks, and coupled release trains in a single codebase.

putItTogether.title: Putting Microservices Decomposition Together
putItTogether.summary: If two services must update state together synchronously on every write, they belong in the same service boundary until you can decouple them with an outbox and asynchronous events.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Microservices Decomposition before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Routing `/api/v2/checkout/*` through Envoy to a standalone Go/PostgreSQL Order service and publishing `OrderPlaced` events via Debezium CDC cut checkout p99 latency from 840 ms to 115 ms and enabled 12x independent daily deploys.
